Avowedly means in a way that has been openly and boldly declared by the person themselves.

When you say someone does something avowedly, you are saying that they themselves have come out and stated it clearly — they haven't hidden it, whispered it, or let others guess. They have put it on the record, publicly and confidently.

Think of it this way: if something is avowedly true about a person, they are the one who said so.

The key ingredient in this word is self-declaration. Not rumour. Not what others observe. Not what is secretly suspected. The person has announced it themselves, without apology or disguise.

"She is avowedly anti-war."

This means: she has openly stated, herself, that she is against war. She hasn't tried to hide or soften it. She owns the label.

"He is avowedly ambitious."

He has declared his ambition openly. He doesn't pretend to be modest about it.

"The organisation is avowedly political."

The organisation itself has made no secret of being political — it has said so plainly.
The Two Things It Always Signals

1. Openness — nothing is being concealed. The declaration is public.

2. Ownership — the subject themselves is the source of the claim. They said it. They stand by it.

These two things together are what make avowedly distinct from just saying something is "known" or "obvious." A person can be obviously nervous, but they haven't avowedly said so. A person can be known to be dishonest, but that's others' judgment. Avowedly always points back to the person's own mouth.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

Openly — just means something is not hidden. It says nothing about who declared it.
"He is openly rude" — you can observe it. He may not have announced it.
"He is avowedly rude" — he has actually said so himself, perhaps even with pride.

Admittedly — carries a tone of reluctance or concession, as if giving something up under pressure.
"Admittedly, the plan failed" — the person is conceding a point, possibly grudgingly.
Avowedly has no such reluctance. It is a confident, willing declaration.

Ostensibly — means appearing to be something, often with a quiet hint that it might not be true underneath.
"Ostensibly, she came to help" — she said she came to help, but maybe she didn't really.
Avowedly is the opposite in spirit — it is sincere and direct self-declaration, not a surface-level cover story.

Purportedly — means something is claimed to be true, but the speaker is slightly doubtful.
"He is purportedly a genius" — someone says so, but we're not sure.
Avowedly does not carry the speaker's doubt. It simply reports that the subject has declared something.

Professedly — the closest synonym to avowedly. Both mean "by one's own declaration." However, professedly can sometimes carry a mild suggestion of doubt (like purportedly), while avowedly tends to be more straightforward and matter-of-fact.
The Situations Where This Word Appears

You will most often see avowedly used when someone:

  • Declares a belief or ideology: "He is an avowedly secular politician."
  • Declares a purpose or intent: "The book is avowedly a work of satire."
  • Declares a personal identity: "She is avowedly feminist."
  • Declares a stance or position: "The company is avowedly against outsourcing."

Notice how in each case, the subject has drawn a clear line and stepped publicly across it. There's a sense of forthrightness — even a quiet boldness — in the word.

Avowedly is a formal word. You will find it in journalism, academic writing, literary criticism, and serious non-fiction. It would sound out of place in casual everyday conversation — you would not typically say "he's avowedly hungry" to a friend. It is reserved for declarations of significance: beliefs, principles, positions, identities, or the declared purpose of a work or institution.
A Quick Test to Know If You've Got It

Before using avowedly, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Has the person (or thing) themselves actually stated or declared this?
  2. Is the declaration open, not hidden?

If the answer to both is yes, then avowedly fits. If the trait is merely observed by others, inferred, or suspected — but not declared — then avowedly is the wrong word.
Avowedly means by one's own open and frank declaration — it signals that the subject themselves has stated something plainly, publicly, and without hiding it.
